messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 63
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Airline Pilot
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 75

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Texture): A specific texture associated with the event, Time of Day: The same time of day the event occurred, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
  Threat: Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
  Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Kavi's Vigil

Kavi Perera was forty-one when the convoy was ambushed near Kandahar. He had been flying transport helicopters for the Australian Defence Force for eight years by then, and he had come to understand the work as a kind of calling—moving supplies, moving people, moving hope into places where it was needed. The morning of the attack, he was waiting on the tarmac for clearance, the rotors already turning, when the radio crackled with a request for emergency extraction from a forward operating base. Three soldiers had been hit. He lifted off without hesitation.

The landing zone was chaos. Dust everywhere, the smell of cordite and something else—something burnt that he would later learn was human tissue. One of the injured men was conscious, his uniform soaked through with blood, and as Kavi's crew loaded him aboard, the man's hand—cold, trembling—grabbed Kavi's wrist. The texture of it stays with him still: the particular roughness of a field dressing soaked through, the specific way a dying man's grip feels when he is trying not to let go of the world. They got airborne. They did not make it to the hospital. The man died in the cabin while Kavi was flying, and for the last thirty seconds of that flight, Kavi had felt the weight of that hand on his wrist even though someone had already pried the fingers away.

Twenty-two years later, Kavi is sixty-three and still flying, though not for the military anymore. He has been with a major American carrier for the last decade, a captain on long-haul routes, and he has built a careful life with his wife Margaret in Portland. To anyone watching him move through an airport or into the cockpit, he appears composed—professional, even. But Kavi has come to understand that he is not the man who boarded that helicopter in 2002. That man is gone, and what remains is something he has come to regard with a kind of horror.

The night vigilance started years ago, so gradually that he did not notice it at first. He would wake at 2:47 a.m.—the exact time the convoy was hit—and lie in the dark, listening. Margaret would be asleep beside him, and he would feel the house around him like a trap, every door and window a potential breach. He had come to believe that darkness was the time when things became real, when the world showed its true nature. During the day, the illusion of safety held. At night, it fell away.

The scanning began during his first year with the American airline. He would enter a cockpit or a briefing room and immediately locate the exits—not consciously, but as an automatic sweep of his eyes before he could attend to anything else. In the cabin, waiting for a flight to board, he would map the space, note where people stood, anticipate sudden movements. When a flight attendant moved too quickly, or when a passenger stood abruptly, Kavi's body would tense, his breath would catch. He was certain that everyone was a potential threat, though he could not articulate why. The world had shown him its teeth once, and he had never stopped waiting for them to close.

The memory itself has become something alien to him—something that belongs to a different person, a different life. When it surfaces, which it does without warning and without mercy, it carries with it the full weight of that original terror. A particular texture—canvas, or certain kinds of fabric, or even the specific roughness of the armrest in the cockpit—can trigger it instantly. The sound of a helicopter, even on television, can send him into a state where he is back on that tarmac, feeling that cold grip on his wrist. The time of day matters too. As 2:47 a.m. approaches, his body knows, and he lies awake, waiting.

Margaret has noticed the changes. She has watched him become someone who is always miserable, who moves through their marriage like a man underwater. He used to laugh easily. He used to be present. Now he is elsewhere, always scanning, always vigilant, always convinced that there is something fundamentally broken inside him—something that marks him as defective, as someone who should not be trusted with the lives of three hundred passengers. The airline has not noticed yet, but Kavi knows they will. He has started making mistakes, small ones, the kind that come from a mind that is never quite here.

It was Margaret who finally insisted he come. She said she could not bear to watch him disappear anymore, and Kavi, sitting in the therapist's office now, can only agree. He does not know if anything can fix what he is, but he has run out of ways to hide it.
